title: Three-Property Rule Strategy
name: Three-Property Rule Strategy
metaTitle: Three-Property Rule Strategy in Phoenix, AZ
metaDescription: Using the three-property identification rule on a Phoenix 1031 exchange, with real candidate examples across industrial, multifamily, and retail.

sections.html: The three-property rule is the simplest identification path in a 1031 exchange: name up to three properties, any value, and move forward. Simple doesn't mean easy to get right, especially when the three candidates span different asset types.

sections.heading: The Rule in Plain Terms
sections.html: Under this rule you can identify up to three replacement properties regardless of their combined value, as opposed to the two-hundred-percent rule, which caps combined value, or the ninety-five-percent rule, which requires closing on most of what's identified. For an investor with one relinquished property and a clear idea of what they want next, three is often enough.

sections.heading: Why This Fits a Lot of Phoenix Exchanges
sections.html: An investor selling one Phoenix asset and rolling into a similar single replacement, say a West Valley industrial building or a multifamily property, usually only needs a short list of two or three real candidates rather than a long backup list. The rule keeps the identification simple when the strategy itself is simple.

sections.heading: Building a Three-Property List That Actually Works
sections.html:
We build these lists with a specific order of priority, not three equally-weighted options:

  • A primary candidate that's already under serious consideration and financeable
  • A close backup in the same asset class in case the primary falls through in diligence
  • A third candidate in a different asset class as a genuine fallback, not padding

That third slot is the one investors most often waste on a property they were never really going to buy. We push to make it a real option instead.

sections.heading: Where This Rule Runs Into Trouble
sections.html: The rule caps you at three named properties no matter their value, so if your relinquished property sold for a large sum and you're eyeing several smaller Phoenix properties to diversify into, this rule may box you in faster than the two-hundred-percent rule would. That's a conversation to have with your qualified intermediary before you commit to using the three-property approach.

sections.heading: Keeping This Aligned With Your Timeline
sections.html:
All three candidates need to be named in writing to your qualified intermediary before the forty-five-day window closes, and you still have one hundred eighty days total to close on whichever one you move forward with. We underwrite all three candidates up front so the choice on day forty-five is a real decision, not a guess.

Which identification rule fits your exchange is a decision for you, your qualified intermediary, and your tax advisor, based on your full situation. We source and rank candidates to match the rule you've chosen.

sections.heading: A Real Three-Property List From a Phoenix Exchange
sections.html:
On one exchange we worked, an investor sold a small retail building and wanted a single replacement. The three-property list carried a net lease pad on Baseline Road as the primary candidate, since it was already under a signed purchase contract in progress, a similar net lease pad on Bell Road as a close backup in case financing on the first fell through, and a small industrial condo unit near Loop 303 as the third slot, chosen specifically because the investor could actually see themselves closing on it if both retail options failed.

The primary candidate closed without needing the backups, but naming all three in writing meant the investor had real options on the table rather than a single point of failure.

sections.heading: When to Consider a Different Rule Instead
sections.html: If your strategy involves splitting proceeds across several smaller Phoenix properties rather than rolling into one, the three-property cap can work against you fast, since a fourth good candidate simply can't go on the list under this rule. That's usually the point where the two-hundred-percent rule, which allows more candidates but caps their combined value, becomes worth discussing with your qualified intermediary instead.

sections.heading: How We Rank Candidates for This Rule Specifically
sections.html: Because this rule only leaves room for three names, we spend more diligence time up front confirming that each candidate is genuinely closable rather than simply available. That means a financing conversation with a lender before the candidate goes on the list, not after, so a property doesn't take one of your three slots only to fall out over a loan that was never going to fund.

sections.heading: What We Send You Before You Sign the Identification Notice
sections.html: Before the notice goes to your qualified intermediary, we send you a short comparison of the three candidates: price, financing status, and what has to happen for each to actually close on schedule. Reviewing that side by side, in writing, catches mismatched expectations before the deadline rather than after it.

faqs.q: How is the three-property rule different from the two-hundred-percent rule?
faqs.a: The three-property rule caps the number of candidates at three regardless of value, while the two-hundred-percent rule allows more candidates but caps their combined value. Which one fits depends on your relinquished sale price and strategy.

faqs.q: Is the three-property rule the right choice if I'm rolling into one Phoenix property?
faqs.a: Often, yes, since a simple one-for-one replacement usually only needs a short, well-ranked candidate list. We still recommend a genuine backup rather than naming only one property.

faqs.q: What happens if all three of my identified properties fall through?
faqs.a: If none of the three closes within the exchange timeline, the exchange generally doesn't complete as planned. That's why we push for candidates that are actually financeable and available, not aspirational picks.

faqs.q: Can my three identified properties span different asset types?
faqs.a: Yes, nothing in the rule requires the same asset class. Some investors use the third slot as a genuine fallback in a different property type, like retail alongside two industrial candidates.

faqs.q: Who decides which identification rule applies to my exchange?
faqs.a: That decision sits with you, your qualified intermediary, and your tax advisor based on your full exchange picture. We build and rank candidate lists to fit whichever rule you've chosen.
